sections.title: Level 2 Mixture Strategy
sections.content: In Level 2 problems, multiple steps and formulas are used. Step 1: Identify the type of problem (Replacement, Alligation, Profit integration). Step 2: Write the required formula or rule. Step 3: Substitute the values. Step 4: Calculate the final ratio or quantity and verify the answer.

sections.title: Repeated Replacement Method
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the total volume V. Step 2: Identify the quantity removed each time (x). Step 3: Identify how many times replacement occurs (n). Step 4: Apply the formula: Final quantity = Initial quantity × (1 - x/V)^n. Step 5: Calculate the remaining amount of the original substance. Example: From 20L of milk, if 5L is removed and replaced with water twice, remaining milk = 20 × (1 - 5/20)^2 = 20 × (3/4)^2.

sections.title: Three Quantity Mixing
sections.content: Step 1: Write the three prices (Cheap, Medium, Dear). Step 2: Apply alligation between the first two prices. Step 3: Combine the result with the third price using the mean price. Step 4: Find the final mixing ratio. Example: To mix ₹50, ₹60, and ₹75 at a mean price of ₹65, first apply alligation between ₹50 and ₹75 and then combine the result with ₹60.

sections.title: Profit and Mixture Integration
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the selling price and profit percentage. Step 2: Calculate the cost price of the mixture using the formula: CP = SP × 100 / (100 + Profit%). Step 3: Treat this CP as the mean price and apply the alligation rule. Step 4: Find the mixing ratio. Example: If the mixture is sold at ₹120/kg with a 20% profit, then CP = 120 × 100 / 120 = ₹100.

sections.title: Mixture Price Balance Concept
sections.content: Step 1: The mean price always lies between the cheap and dear prices. Step 2: The distance from the mean determines the ratio. Step 3: The price closer to the mean will have a larger quantity. Step 4: Simplify the ratio.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Forgetting to apply the power n in repeated replacement. 2. Taking the wrong mean price. 3. Applying alligation without first calculating CP in profit problems. 4. Forgetting to simplify the ratio.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Level 2 mixture problems involve the replacement formula, multi-alligation, and profit integration. Identifying the correct formula and applying the steps in the correct order is the key to solving these questions.

tricks.title: Replacement Power Trick
tricks.explanation: In repeated replacement problems, always use the formula (1 - x/V)^n.
tricks.example: From a 30L mixture, removing 5L three times → Remaining = Initial × (1 - 5/30)^3.

tricks.title: Quick Fraction Simplification
tricks.explanation: Simplify the fraction first when using the replacement formula.

tricks.title: Three Price Shortcut
tricks.explanation: First combine the extreme prices, then mix the result with the middle price.
tricks.example: ₹40, ₹50, ₹70 → First find the ratio of ₹40 and ₹70.

tricks.title: Profit to CP Shortcut
tricks.explanation: Quickly calculate CP from selling price and profit percentage.

tricks.title: Mean Distance Rule
tricks.explanation: The distance from the mean determines the mixing ratio.

tricks.title: Power Pattern Trick
tricks.explanation: Repeated replacement follows a geometric decrease pattern.
tricks.example: At each step, the original substance is multiplied by (1 - x/V).

tricks.title: Cheap More Rule
tricks.explanation: If the mean price is closer to the cheaper price, the cheaper ingredient will be in larger quantity.
tricks.example: ₹40 and ₹80 with mean ₹50 → Quantity of ₹40 will be higher.

tricks.title: Final Price Check
tricks.explanation: The final mixture price must always lie between the original prices.
